primer.jpn_p_world.title: Land of the Rising Sun
primer.jpn_p_world.text: You were born in Nippon, 'the land where the sun rises'. In Kyoto lives the emperor, believed to descend from the sun goddess Amaterasu, but it is not he who rules: power lies with the shogun, the supreme general, and his samurai vassals. Over these four centuries Japan will pass from the war of the Taira and Minamoto clans, through the age of the shoguns, to a century when everyone fights everyone. By rough estimates some ten million people live on the islands, and nearly all of them grow rice.
primer.jpn_p_world_kamakura.title: The Kamakura Shogunate
primer.jpn_p_world_kamakura.text: You were born in the Kamakura age. From 1180 to 1185 the Taira and Minamoto clans fought for power until the Taira fleet perished at Dan-no-ura. Minamoto no Yoritomo became shogun and set up his headquarters at Kamakura; after his death the country is run by regents of the Hojo family. In 1221 the retired emperor Go-Toba tried to restore power to the court and lost. In 1274 and 1281 Mongol fleets came, and both times, it is said, a divine wind – kamikaze – scattered them.
primer.jpn_p_world_muromachi.title: The Ashikaga Shoguns
primer.jpn_p_world_muromachi.text: You were born under the Ashikaga shoguns. In 1333 Kamakura fell and Emperor Go-Daigo tried to rule in person, but within three years the general Ashikaga Takauji put another emperor on the throne and became shogun himself. Until 1392 there are two courts: the Northern in Kyoto and the Southern in the mountains of Yoshino. The shogun's headquarters stands in Kyoto's Muromachi district. The shogun Yoshimitsu built the Golden Pavilion and trades with Ming China.
primer.jpn_p_world_sengoku.title: The Warring States
primer.jpn_p_world_sengoku.text: You were born in the Sengoku age, the age of 'warring provinces'. The Onin War of 1467 to 1477 burned Kyoto, and the shogun now rules almost only on paper. The land is carved up by daimyo, lords who raise their own armies and write their own laws. People call it gekokujo, 'the low overthrow the high': vassals kill their masters, and peasants seize whole provinces. In 1543 the Portuguese brought the first guns to the island of Tanegashima.
primer.jpn_p_world_unification.title: The Unifiers
primer.jpn_p_world_unification.text: You were born as the country is being forged together by an iron hand. In 1568 Oda Nobunaga marched into Kyoto; he burned the monastery of Enryakuji and in 1573 drove out the last Ashikaga shogun. After his death at Honno-ji temple in 1582, his work passed to Toyotomi Hideyoshi, the son of a common foot soldier. Hideyoshi took the swords from the peasants, surveyed every field and twice sent armies into Korea. In 1600 Tokugawa Ieyasu will win at Sekigahara.
primer.jpn_p_world_echigo.title: The Uesugi Lords
primer.jpn_p_world_echigo.text: You were born in Echigo, ruled by a famous warrior. Nagao Kagetora has held the province since 1548, and in 1561 he takes the name Uesugi; later he will be known as Kenshin. He worships Bishamon, god of war, and meets Takeda Shingen five times on the plain of Kawanakajima. They say he once sent his enemy salt when Takeda was cut off from the sea. After Kenshin dies in 1578 his adopted sons fight over the inheritance, and in 1598 Hideyoshi moves the Uesugi to distant Aizu.
primer.jpn_p_society.title: Court, Warriors, Temples
primer.jpn_p_society.text: Three powers stand at the top: the court nobles, kuge, around the emperor; the warriors, buke, around the shogun; and the great temples with their own lands and even their own warrior monks. They own the estates, shoen, which are worked by peasants called hyakusho. Craftsmen and merchants form guilds, za, under the patronage of temples and nobles. At the bottom are those deemed 'impure': hinin and kawaramono, 'riverbank people'. Others shun them, though among them are garden designers and actors.
primer.jpn_p_society_slave.title: Genin
primer.jpn_p_society_slave.text: You were born to a family of genin, bonded servants. People become genin through debt, in famine years when they sell themselves or their children, or in war, when soldiers carry off captives and sell them. Genin work in the house and the fields and can be sold, given away or handed over as dowry. In the later sixteenth century the Portuguese buy Japanese people and ship them overseas, until in 1587 Hideyoshi forbids selling people to foreigners.
primer.jpn_p_society_peasant.title: Hyakusho
primer.jpn_p_society_peasant.text: You were born to a farming family, hyakusho, 'the hundred names'. From the fields goes nengu, the rice tax, sometimes as much as half the crop, plus labour for the lord. But the village is not defenceless: self-governing communities called so settle their own affairs, share out water and keep order. When debts choke them, peasants band together in leagues, ikki: in 1428 they sacked moneylenders right outside the capital, and in Kaga province followers of the Ikko sect governed themselves for over ninety years.
primer.jpn_p_society_samurai.title: A Samurai House
primer.jpn_p_society_samurai.text: You were born into a samurai family. The word samurai means 'one who serves': for his lord's favour – land, or the income from it – the warrior pays with service and blood. The shogun's vassals are called gokenin and serve as estate stewards, jito. The old name for the warrior's path was 'the way of bow and horse'; the word bushido does not exist yet and will be celebrated later. Land is split among heirs, and a poor samurai ploughs his own field beside the peasants.
primer.jpn_p_society_noble.title: A Noble House
primer.jpn_p_society_noble.text: You were born into a noble house. The court families, kuge – Konoe, Kujo, Saionji and others – have served the emperor for centuries and know the ceremonies, the poetry and the ancient robes. But power and land keep slipping to the warriors, and in troubled times many a courtier sells his calligraphy to make ends meet. The new nobility are the daimyo, lords of provinces, with castles, thousands of warriors and marriages that seal alliances.
primer.jpn_p_birth.title: The Birthing Hut
primer.jpn_p_birth.text: Childbirth is considered a source of pollution, so a separate hut, ubuya, is often built for it, or a special room set aside. In the fifth month of pregnancy the mother ties a white sash, iwata-obi, around her belly for luck. On the seventh night after birth the child is named, and about a month later it is carried to the shrine to be shown to the local guardian god. In noble houses a bowstring is twanged during the birth to drive away evil spirits. Boys' childhood names often end in '-maru'.
primer.jpn_p_childhood.title: Children and Temples
primer.jpn_p_childhood.text: Little children ride on the backs of older brothers and sisters, and from five or six they help out: scaring birds from the rice fields, gathering firewood, minding the younger ones. Those who are to learn to read are sent to a temple, where boys copy sutras and learn to write from a primer called Teikin Orai. At twelve to fifteen a boy undergoes genpuku, the coming-of-age rite: his hair is tied up, he is given an eboshi cap and an adult name.
primer.jpn_p_childhood_samurai.title: A Warrior's Son
primer.jpn_p_childhood_samurai.text: A samurai's son is put on a horse and handed a bow almost as soon as he can walk. In the Kamakura age youths practised shooting from the saddle at moving targets; later they learn the spear and the sword. He memorises the names and deeds of his ancestors, bows to his lord and learns who the family's enemies are. At thirteen to fifteen comes genpuku: a patron sets the eboshi cap on his head and gives him part of his own name. In the Sengoku age many sons are sent to allies as hostages.
primer.jpn_p_home.title: Hearth and Thatch
primer.jpn_p_home.text: A farmhouse is a timber frame under a thick thatched roof. Half the house is a beaten-earth floor for cooking and work, half a raised plank floor with straw mats. In the middle is the irori hearth, with a pot hanging from a hook above it, and the smoke escapes straight through the roof. Sliding doors of paper and wood, and tatami mats covering the whole floor, appear in wealthy homes in the Muromachi age. There is hardly any furniture: people sit and sleep on the floor.
primer.jpn_p_food.title: Rice and Miso
primer.jpn_p_food.text: Rice is the heart of every meal, but the poor eat it mixed with millet or barley, or millet alone. With it come miso soup, pickles, seaweed, fish and vegetables. Buddhism frowns on the meat of domestic animals, but game and fish are eaten gladly. People usually eat twice a day. The monk Eisai, it is believed, brought tea seeds from China in 1191 and wrote that tea heals, and tofu came with the Zen monks. People drink sake, rice wine.
primer.jpn_p_clothes.title: Kosode and Eboshi
primer.jpn_p_clothes.text: Ordinary people wear hemp and ramie; cotton will only be grown here from the sixteenth century. The kosode, a robe with short sleeves and ancestor of the kimono, is becoming the main garment. Samurai wear the hitatare and wide hakama trousers. A grown man never goes out bareheaded: he wears an eboshi cap. Noble women wear their hair down to their heels and blacken their teeth – a custom called ohaguro, which court men follow too.
primer.jpn_p_faith.title: Gods and Buddhas
primer.jpn_p_faith.text: In Japan the kami – gods of mountains, rivers and ancestors – live side by side with the buddhas. Many believe the kami are local forms of buddhas, and temples often stand beside shrines. New schools of Buddhism arose in these centuries: Honen and Shinran taught that simply repeating the name of Amida Buddha brings salvation, Nichiren championed the Lotus Sutra, and Eisai and Dogen brought Zen from China. Almost every family visits both shrine and temple.
primer.jpn_p_faith_buddhist.title: Namu Amida Butsu
primer.jpn_p_faith_buddhist.text: Your family holds to Buddhism. Followers of the Pure Land repeat 'Namu Amida Butsu', hoping to be reborn after death in Amida's paradise; Nichiren's disciples beat drums and chant 'Namu Myoho Renge Kyo'; Zen monks sit for hours in silence. Great monasteries like Enryakuji on Mount Hiei keep their own warrior monks. Memorial services are held for the dead, and in summer, at the Bon festival, the souls of the ancestors are welcomed home with fires.
primer.jpn_p_faith_shinto.title: The Way of the Gods
primer.jpn_p_faith_shinto.text: Your family honours the kami, the gods who dwell in mountains, trees and springs and in shrines behind red torii gates. Before praying you rinse your hands and mouth and clap; at matsuri festivals the gods ride through the streets in noisy processions of portable shrines. The worst thing is kegare, pollution from death, blood or illness, washed away by purification rites. Your village shrine is home to its guardian, the ujigami, and every newborn is under its care. Many dream of one day making the pilgrimage to Ise, shrine of the sun goddess Amaterasu.
primer.jpn_p_faith_catholic.title: Kirishitan
primer.jpn_p_faith_catholic.text: Your family has accepted the Kirishitan teaching, the Christianity brought in 1549 by the Jesuit Francis Xavier. God is called Deusu; people carry rosaries and small crosses and pray in 'southern barbarian temples'. Lords were baptised too: in 1580 Omura Sumitada even gave the port of Nagasaki to the Jesuits. By 1600 there are perhaps three hundred thousand Christians. But in 1587 Hideyoshi ordered the missionaries to leave, and in 1597 twenty-six Christians were executed at Nagasaki.
primer.jpn_p_work.title: Markets and Copper
primer.jpn_p_work.text: Japan mints almost no coins of its own: people use Chinese copper cash, first Song coins and later Ming 'Eiraku tsuho'. Rice remains the measure of wealth, and after Hideyoshi's land survey the yield of land is counted in koku of rice. Markets meet three times a month, and in the Muromachi age six. Craftsmen and traders form guilds, za: the oil merchants of Yamazaki, for example, serve the Hachiman shrine. Sake brewers and owners of stone storehouses lend money at interest, and Nobunaga opens free markets without guilds.
primer.jpn_p_place.title: The Islands
primer.jpn_p_place.text: Japan is a chain of mountainous islands where barely a seventh of the land can be farmed, and every valley is a small world of its own. Roads are few, and goods move more easily by sea. Summer brings rains and typhoons; winter buries the western coast in deep snow. Earthquakes shake the ground, and mountains sometimes smoke. There are sixty-six provinces, each with its own dialect, its own lords and its own shrines. The capital is Kyoto, but power belongs more and more to whoever holds the castles in the provinces.
primer.jpn_p_place_kyoto.title: The Capital
primer.jpn_p_place_kyoto.text: Kyoto, the ancient Heian-kyo, is laid out in a grid of streets on the Chinese model, between mountains and the Kamo River. Here stand the emperor's palace, hundreds of temples, the Golden Pavilion and later the Silver one. The city has burned many times, worst of all in the Onin War, which left whole quarters in ashes. Yet the townspeople, machishu, rebuild every time, and in 1500 they bring the Gion festival's giant floats back onto the streets. Workshops in the Nishijin quarter weave the finest silk in the land.
primer.jpn_p_place_kamakura.title: City of Warriors
primer.jpn_p_place_kamakura.text: Kamakura is squeezed between hills and Sagami Bay, and seven narrow passes cut through the rock lead into the city. Above it stands the Tsurugaoka Hachiman shrine, home of the Minamoto clan's guardian god, and from 1252 a giant bronze Buddha more than eleven metres tall is cast here. The Hojo regents build the Zen monasteries of Kenchoji and Engakuji. Samurai from all over the country come here to argue their land suits. In 1333 the troops of Nitta Yoshisada will storm the city and burn it.
primer.jpn_p_place_hakata.title: Gateway to the Mainland
primer.jpn_p_place_hakata.text: Hakata on Kyushu is the port closest to China and Korea. Chinese merchants live here, and in 1195 the monk Eisai founded Shofukuji, Japan's first Zen temple. After the first Mongol invasion a stone wall some twenty kilometres long was built along the bay. In summer bearers race shouting through the streets with huge decorated floats; tradition says the festival began in 1241, when a monk drove out a plague.
primer.jpn_p_place_sakai.title: The Free City
primer.jpn_p_place_sakai.text: Sakai is ringed by a water-filled moat, and it is ruled not by a lord but by a council of rich merchants, the egoshu. Ships sail from here to China, guns are forged here, and in 1561 the missionary Vilela compared the city to Venice. The tea master Sen no Rikyu was born in Sakai. But freedom does not last: in 1568 Nobunaga demanded twenty thousand strings of coins from the city, and the merchants had to submit.
primer.jpn_p_place_echigo.title: Snow Country
primer.jpn_p_place_echigo.text: Echigo lies on the Sea of Japan, and in winter the wind off the sea buries its houses in snow up to the eaves. In spring the snow melts and waters the rice fields, of which there are many. The province is famous for ramie fibre and cloth, aoso, carried to the capital for sale. In 1207 the monk Shinran was exiled here, and here, it is thought, he married – unheard of for a monk. On a mountain above the coast stands Kasugayama castle.
primer.jpn_p_law.title: Courts and Punishment
primer.jpn_p_law.text: In 1232 the Hojo regents drew up the Goseibai Shikimoku, 51 articles on land, inheritance and service, and samurai travel to Kamakura to sue for their estates. In the Sengoku age every daimyo writes his own laws, and many punish both parties to a brawl without asking who was right. In disputed cases people sometimes plunge a hand into boiling water, believing the gods will protect the innocent. Executions are cruel – crucifixion, and in 1594 the bandit Ishikawa Goemon was reportedly boiled alive in a cauldron.
primer.jpn_p_health.title: Plague and Famine
primer.jpn_p_health.text: Smallpox, measles, dysentery and fevers come in waves, and families often bury children. Worst of all is famine: in 1460 and 1461 crop failure and war ravaged the land, and in Kyoto, by one monk's count, 82,000 people died in two months. Healing means Chinese herbs, needles and moxa burned on the skin; doctors are often monks, and in the sixteenth century Manase Dosan opened a school of medicine in Kyoto. In 1557 the Portuguese set up a hospital in Funai.
primer.jpn_p_women.title: Wife and Mistress
primer.jpn_p_women.text: In the Kamakura age a woman can inherit land and even serve as an estate steward, and Yoritomo's widow, Hojo Masako, ruled as the 'nun shogun'. Over time, though, land passes only to the eldest son, and a wife moves for good into her husband's house. Daimyo daughters are married off to seal alliances. Ordinary women work the fields, brew sake and trade in markets, and the women of Ohara carry bundles of firewood into the capital on their heads.
primer.jpn_p_leisure.title: Noh and Tea
primer.jpn_p_leisure.text: In summer, at the Bon festival, the whole village dances; in spring people admire the cherry blossom. Blind monks with the biwa lute chant the Tale of the Heike. Under Yoshimitsu the actors Kan'ami and Zeami created Noh theatre – masks, flute and drums – with comic kyogen plays between the pieces. Nobles compose chains of linked verse, renga, and kick the kemari ball. In the sixteenth century the tea gathering comes into fashion, and Sen no Rikyu turns it into an art of simplicity.
primer.jpn_p_knowledge.title: Writing and Books
primer.jpn_p_knowledge.text: The Japanese write with Chinese characters and with their own syllabic script, kana. Zen monks of the Five Mountains compose poetry in Chinese, and in the eastern province of Shimotsuke stands the Ashikaga school, which Xavier called the greatest university in Japan. These centuries produced the Tale of the Heike, Kamo no Chomei's 'An Account of My Hut' and the monk Kenko's 'Essays in Idleness'. In 1590 the Jesuits will bring a printing press with movable type.
primer.jpn_p_war.title: Bow and Horse
primer.jpn_p_war.text: The Kamakura samurai is above all a mounted archer. Before battle he calls out his name and lineage, challenging a worthy opponent. His armour of lacquered plates laced with silk cords weighs around twenty-five kilos. The Mongols surprised the Japanese in 1274: they fought in formation rather than man to man, and hurled exploding bombs. For ordinary people the worst of war is not the battles but the looting and fires that come with every army.
primer.jpn_p_war_sengoku.title: Spears and Guns
primer.jpn_p_war_sengoku.text: In the Sengoku age wars are no longer fought by handfuls of noble horsemen but by thousands of ashigaru, foot soldiers from the peasantry armed with long spears. Castles rise on the hills, and after 1543 smiths in Sakai and Kunitomo forge tanegashima guns; soon, it is said, Japan has as many as some European countries. At Nagashino in 1575 Nobunaga's gunners broke the Takeda cavalry; the famous three-rank volleys may be a later legend.
